description: Dusk Orbit is a one-person team from Adana, Türkiye, at the Niğde local event. I'm working on the Dancing with the SARs challenge: using NASA-ISRO's new NISAR radar satellite to find out what changed in the farmland near my home after the first autumn rain, then testing the answer at random places around the world. Interests: Earth observation, data analysis and clear design. This is a solo team, so I'm not looking for new members.
summary:
Rain fools radar. Between Passes shows what really changed.

Satellites find floods, harvests and cut-down forests by comparing two pictures of the same place. But rain fools them: wet ground looks different, so after a rainy week whole regions look "changed" when nothing happened. I measured this with NASA-ISRO's new NISAR radar: at 147 random places, 28 times more land looked "changed" where NASA's SMAP satellite saw the soil get wetter or drier.

Between Passes is a filter that sorts out those false alarms, so people see only the real changes. Wetter soil can only brighten radar and drier soil only darken it, so a change that goes against the weather must be real. It is built for disaster teams looking for floods, agencies watching farms and forests, and farmers checking their fields. The free web app covers 148 places in 39 countries; one command runs it anywhere NISAR has flown.

In my home region, Ceyhan in southern Türkiye, it lists the fields the first autumn rain can't explain. With rules written first, I showed worldwide, twice, that NISAR tracks soil moisture, and I published predictions for three upcoming passes before NASA released the data.
details:
What it does

Between Passes is a weather filter for radar change maps. NISAR compares two passes 12 days apart and flags what changed. But soil moisture changes radar strongly: wetter soil looks brighter, drier soil darker. Between Passes reads NASA SMAP soil moisture and NASA POWER rain for the same days and sorts every change into "could be the weather" and "beyond the weather". The free web app (no login, works on a phone) lets you:

- watch the filter work on real NISAR radar over Ceyhan, Türkiye, in three steps;

- explore 148 places in 39 countries on a world map; each place has a card where you drag between the two passes, switch the filter on, and share a link;

- see Ceyhan's "where to look first" list: the fields that got darker while the soil got wetter, with the nearest village;

- follow a guided tour in the Ceyhan lab: tap any of 636 changed fields, draw your own field and measure it live, export the evidence;

- check three predictions that score themselves as NASA releases the data;

- read a Turkish page for local farmers.

A command (scripts/bp_check.py --lat --lon) runs the whole filter on any place NISAR has flown, with a free Earthdata account.

How it works

1. Find: NASA's catalogue gives two NISAR L2 GCOV passes over a point on the identical orbit and grid, so no resampling is needed.

2. Read: the code downloads only the needed window of each 1.9 GB file (about 70 MB) over HTTP.

3. Measure: change of 3 dB or more (twice or half the radar echo), after a 100 m speckle filter. At Ceyhan the town centre, which should not change, moved only 0.12 dB.

4. Ask the weather: SMAP soil moisture on both days and POWER rain in between.

5. Sort: a change in the direction the soil moisture moved could be the weather; a change against it, or any change where the soil stayed the same, is beyond the weather. The rules were committed to GitHub before running them.

6. Prove the physics: with the test plan committed first, at 74 random NISAR sites worldwide radar change tracked SMAP soil-moisture change: a strong link with less than a 1-in-1,000 chance of being luck (Spearman ρ = 0.58, p < 0.001); a repeat on 73 new random sites gave ρ = 0.55, p < 0.001.

7. Predict: if Ceyhan's 508 brightened fields were wet soil, they will dim as it dries. I locked predictions for three upcoming passes (from three orbits) on GitHub before NASA released the data; the app scores them with code saved in advance.

8. Verify: 37 automated tests, and the browser recomputes the published numbers from the shipped data on every load.

Results

Where the soil got wetter or drier, a median 5.0% of the land changed by 3 dB or more, against 0.18% where it stayed the same (28×); pooled, 85% of that "change" could be the weather alone. Of 147 random places, 41 show real change beyond the weather, 26 mostly weather, 80 quiet. At Ceyhan, 88% of the changed land could be the rain; 128 fields that got darker could not, and an optical satellite (NASA HLS) shows only 9% of the brightened fields lost their plants.

Benefits and impact

Anyone who uses radar change maps (disaster responders mapping floods, agencies watching farmland or forests, insurers, researchers) has to separate weather from real change. Between Passes shows how to do that with free NASA data and gives a ranked list of where to look. For Çukurova, one of Türkiye's main farming plains, it tells a farmer or inspector which fields really changed after the first autumn rain, through cloud, every 12 days.

What makes it creative

Most projects stop at a colourful change map. This one asks which changes are only weather, answers with three other NASA missions, proves the physics at random places with rules written in advance, and commits to predictions before the data exist.

What I considered

It is a screening filter, not a cause detector: it says where to look, not what happened. SMAP measures 9 km cells, so a local shower can look like real change; 63% of randomly picked sites lacked a quality SMAP reading; Ceyhan's SMAP comparison uses a labelled ±2-day window. All limits are stated in the app and the repository. Accessibility: no login, no installation, phone-friendly, Turkish page.

Tools

Python (h5py, NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, Shapely, Pillow, requests, pytest); a static web app in HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no framework or server; GitHub Actions and Pages; OpenStreetMap and Natural Earth for map context.

AI use: The project idea, research question, study area and every key decision are mine. AI (Claude Code) wrote the code, ran the data analysis and drafted the documents, and suggested methods and wording that I reviewed and chose to use.
